hypothesis.title: The Hidden Bands of Form
hypothesis.question: Can a musical identity be carried by separable planning, harmonic-geometry, spectral-signature, and dialogic-surface bands rather than by foreground notes alone?
hypothesis.hypothesis: If a 90-second study is built with four independently controlled bands—semantic plan, adjacency-governed harmony, subtle spectral signature, and timbral call-and-response—then ablating each band will selectively weaken a different perceived quality: overall form, harmonic inevitability, identity under filtering, or dialogue. The reason is that the selected sources all show structure distributed across bands or layers that must later be fused: frequency bands in bioacoustics, abstraction bands in video-to-music generation, phase/log-magnitude carrier bands in watermarking, combinatorial geometry bands in harmony, accessible phase paths in ice, and dialogic production layers in electronic music.
hypothesis.rationaleMd: S3 shows that inherited baseband audio pipelines can discard meaningful high-frequency bioacoustic information, while multi-band decomposition and fusion recovers structure. S4 separates high-level semantic planning from low-level diffusion synthesis, giving a planning/rendering band split. S5 demonstrates that STFT phase bins and adjacent log-magnitude differences can carry robust hidden signatures without dominating perception. S2 formalizes harmonic resources through combinatorial configurations, making adjacency a structural band beneath named chords. S1 grounds the idea physically: large possibility spaces only realize forms through accessible transition paths. S6 gives the practical studio surface: timbral families, phrases, and silence answer one another across arrangement layers. Together they support a band-aware composition experiment in which each layer carries a different aspect of form [S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, S6].

recipe.title: Multi-Band Signature Piece
recipe.bodyMd: Create a 90-second study at 96 BPM with four independently designed bands. First, write a planning band: a short verbal or symbolic plan with three sections, such as question, false fusion, real fusion [S4]. Second, create a harmonic geometry band: choose a small Tonnetz-like graph or 6–8 chord adjacency map and allow harmony to move only to adjacent states, preferring nearest-accessible moves except at high-pressure section boundaries [S1, S2]. Third, create a spectral signature band: a subtle high-band or phase-like recurring layer such as seeded narrow EQ boosts above 6 kHz, a noise contour, or a phase-smear gesture; render an alternate version with an 8 kHz low-pass to test identity loss [S3, S5]. Fourth, create a dialogic surface band: two timbral families, such as sampled texture and analog-modeled bass, answer each other with phrases and silence [S6]. Render four ablations—full fusion, no signature, no geometry, and no plan—and blind-rate identity, inevitability, and dialogue.

parameters.value: four bands with four ablation renders

dawChecklist: Write a three-section verbal/symbolic plan before sound design: question, false fusion, real fusion.
Draw a 6–8 node chord adjacency graph and restrict harmonic movement to adjacent nodes.
Design a subtle spectral signature above roughly 6 kHz using seeded EQ, noise contour, cymbal phase smear, or similar high-band material.
Create two contrasting timbral families and arrange them in call-and-response, including at least two silent answers.
Render Full Fusion with all four bands active.
Render No Signature by removing or 8 kHz low-pass filtering the spectral signature layer.
Render No Geometry by keeping the same sounds but allowing arbitrary chord movement.
Render No Plan by keeping local materials but randomizing section order.
Blind-rate the four renders for identity, inevitability, and dialogue on a 1–7 scale.

protocol.listeningContext: studio headphones, matched integrated loudness before rating
protocol.listeningMethod: blind shuffled comparison with 1–7 ratings for identity, inevitability, and dialogue
